Definition: Percentage of the national population covered by at least one 4G/LTE mobile network signal, whether or not they subscribe to the service. 4G is the practical minimum for meaningful broadband connectivity enabling digital services.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. ITU DataHub gives 32.2% population coverage (2024); a 2024 peer-reviewed study citing the national regulator ARCT gives 32% (Dec 2022); a 2025 secondary report citing the same ARCT data gives 32% (2023). All fall within the 25-49% bracket, matching the original code 2. The original single, older World Bank source (25%, 2019) is superseded by these newer, mutually corroborating figures, but the bracket — and therefore the code — is unchanged.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Comments: 1 IXP BurundiX, 9 members, moderate participation. [[Internet Society Pulse](https://pulse.internetsociety.org/en/ixp-tracker/country/BI/)]
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and now corroborated by three independent sources. Internet Society Pulse and PeeringDB both record BDIXP (Bujumbura) with 9 members/peers and c.26 Gbps total capacity; the operator's own site (bdixp.org.bi) reports 10 active members, 7.5 Gbps peak traffic and 99.9% uptime, with members including Akamai, Meta and PCH route servers. This is a single, moderately active exchange consistent with code 4; code unchanged.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited source itself states 36.8% unique mobile subscribers (c.2019-20), which falls in the 25-39% bracket (code 2) under this variable's scale, not the 55-69% bracket (code 4) that was recorded — the original coding does not match its own cited evidence. No fresher country-specific GSMA unique-subscriber figure for Burundi was found; more recent World Bank/GSMA data (56.6-63.2%, 2022-2025) measure SIM 'connections'/subscriptions, a different (higher) metric than unique subscribers, and the Sub-Saharan Africa regional unique-subscriber average was still only c.44% in 2023 (GSMA Mobile Economy SSA 2024). Corrected to code 2 to match the scale and the only authoritative unique-subscriber figure found; flagged for human review as the true current unique-subscriber rate may have risen and merits a fresh GSMA Intelligence country snapshot if one becomes available.

Definition: Whether the government has established dedicated data center infrastructure and/or a government cloud (G-Cloud) strategy for hosting e-government services and public sector data domestically. Critical for data sovereignty and e-government service delivery.
Value Name: Government data center planned or under construction
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original 2020 source (a purchase of Russian 'MyOffice' office software) is unrelated to government data centre or cloud strategy and should not have been cited for this variable. Better evidence: the World Bank-financed PAFEN programme (2023-2028, US$92m) explicitly includes establishing a national data centre and modernising the government's shared network/hosting infrastructure; as of the March 2026 mid-term review this remains a stated priority still being implemented (project site rehabilitation under way; data centre not yet operational). This still corresponds to code 2 (planned/under construction), so the code is confirmed but on entirely different, corrected grounds — the original source should be replaced.

Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
Value Name: Basic policy exists but limited implementation
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: A new electricity law passed in March 2024 creates a legal framework for private-sector-led mini-grid and off-grid development (concessions/licences); a dedicated rural electrification agency (ABER) and subsidy fund (FESEC) are financing off-grid access for c.70,000 households and clean cooking for 300,000; a PPP (Weza Power/Anzana Electric Group, agreed Dec 2023) is connecting 45,000 households/businesses; and a new GEF-UNDP mini-grid project was approved in 2025. This is beyond 'basic policy with limited implementation' and better matches code 3 (active policy with some deployment); upgraded from 2 to 3.
